narration: for the copper complex, colourimetry or uv-visible: it's strongly coloured, so it absorbs visible light, best measured at lambda max. for trace lead, graphite-furnace aas: lead is colourless, and the furnace measures far lower levels than a flame. saying aas detects the lead ions in the water is the trap. it measures free atoms.

a century ago, australian doctors still treated children for rickets, where growing bones soften and bend, and scurvy, where gums bleed and wounds won't heal. today, the nutrition-linked diseases that fill our hospitals are mostly type 2 diabetes and heart disease. one set comes from too little. the other is linked to long-term excess, alongside other risk factors. so how does what we eat change disease risk?

take iron. you've seen its chain already: too little iron means less haemoglobin, smaller, paler red cells, and less oxygen carried, which is iron-deficiency anaemia. the nutrition question is why the iron is low. a diet with too little iron, or a gut that absorbs it poorly, makes it a nutritional deficiency. but losing blood, for example from heavy periods or bleeding in the gut, drains iron too, and that cause isn't the diet. so check where the iron went before you call it nutritional.

### 4. vitamin c and vitamin d
> the same chain works for vitamins. vitamin c is needed by the enzymes that build strong collagen, the rope-like protein that holds together gums, skin and blood vessel walls. without it, new collagen is weak, so small vessels leak, gums bleed and wounds heal slowly. that's scurvy. vitamin d lets your gut absorb calcium. without it, growing bones don't harden properly, so they can bend under the body's weight. that's rickets. scurvy has a c in it, for vitamin c. rickets, think vitamin d. your skin can make it in sunlight, and some foods and supplements supply it too.

the nutrient is vitamin d, and its job is helping the gut absorb calcium. with little sunlight, the skin makes little vitamin d, so less calcium is absorbed. growing bone doesn't harden properly and stays soft, so it can bend under the body's weight, which is rickets. the classic mistake is answering "drink more milk". without vitamin d, extra calcium isn't absorbed well.

obesity and a family history both go with higher rates, and together, the highest. but even in the highest group, about thirty in a thousand developed diabetes each year, so most didn't, and some healthy-weight adults did. and the data didn't measure food intake, so they can't show that eating too much caused these cases. the classic mistake is treating a higher rate as a guarantee.

the classic mistake is thinking two thousand people makes the claim proven. more responses can reduce random uncertainty, but don't remove selection bias or fix the design. a snapshot still can't show a cause. for that, you need the order in time, and a way to deal with confounders.

you might expect a taller peak to mean more carbons. not here. only about one carbon atom in a hundred is carbon-13, so two of them are rarely bonded together. the machine is also run so that neighbouring hydrogens can't split the carbon signals, which is called decoupling. so each environment shows as one sharp line. peak heights in carbon-13 aren't reliable counts, so don't read them as ratios. count the lines, and read where they sit.

how strong is the evidence? take direct, a trial in scotland and england. gp practices were randomly assigned. in one group, adults diagnosed in the past six years had a low-energy diet for several months, then support to keep the weight off. other practices gave usual care. after a year, 46 per cent of the diet group were in remission, glucose below the diabetes threshold without glucose-lowering medicines, against 4 per cent with usual care.

a couple of days after birth, nearly every baby born in nsw is offered a heel-prick blood test, checking for more than twenty conditions. one of them, pku, can cause severe brain damage, yet babies found this way can grow up without it. so did the test prevent a genetic disease, or only find it? that's today's question: when can genetics help prevent disease?

genetic technologies do three different jobs. screening finds a risk or a condition, but it doesn't change any dna. embryo testing chooses between embryos that already exist. genetic engineering changes the genetic material itself. so for any method, ask which job it does, and what exactly it prevents: symptoms in a person, the birth of an affected child, or the faulty gene itself.

start with the heel prick. in pku, short for phenylketonuria, both copies of one gene are faulty, so the liver makes too little working enzyme to break down phenylalanine, an amino acid in ordinary protein. phenylalanine builds up in the blood and damages the developing brain. if the test finds it early, the baby starts a low-phenylalanine diet straightaway, the level stays low, and the brain develops normally.

the second job is finding risk before a pregnancy. you've met carriers before: people with one altered allele for a recessive condition like cystic fibrosis, plus one working copy, so they're usually healthy. most don't know it. if two carriers have children, each pregnancy has a one in four chance of an affected child. carrier screening tests a couple before or early in pregnancy, and medicare now funds it for three conditions, including cystic fibrosis.

in the inner ear, the cochlea is a coiled, fluid-filled tube. as the stapes pushes, waves travel through the fluid and make a membrane inside vibrate. high sounds move it most near the start of the coil, and low sounds further along. sitting on that membrane are hair cells, the receptors here. when it moves, their tiny hairs bend, ion channels open, and the cell triggers signals in the auditory nerve, which carries them to the brain. so the cochlea is where vibration becomes a nerve signal.

clear vision needs the eye's bending power to match its length. in myopia, or short-sightedness, the eyeball is usually too long, or the cornea too steeply curved. light from a distant object comes to a point in front of the retina, then spreads out again, so distant things look blurred. light from a near object is already spreading as it arrives, so it focuses further back, on the retina, and near things look clear. to remember it: with myopia, you see what's near "my" eyes.

narration: for a focus fault, change how light is bent before it reaches the retina. glasses do it from outside the eye. for myopia, a concave lens, thinner in the middle, spreads the light a little, moving the focus back onto the retina. for hyperopia and for reading, a convex lens, thicker in the middle, bends light inward, moving the focus forward. for astigmatism, a toric lens bends light differently in different directions. contact lenses do the same job on the cornea, moving with the eye for a wider clear view. but worn overnight or cleaned poorly, they can let an infection into the cornea.

absent: breaks the old lens into small pieces
narration: for a cataract, the fix is to replace the cloudy lens. through a tiny cut, ultrasound breaks up the old lens, and it's removed. a folded artificial lens, made of clear plastic, is slipped in and opens into place. light passes through clearly again, and the new lens can also correct short- or long-sightedness. but it can't change shape, so most people still need reading glasses. there's also a small risk of infection. and it only helps if the retina still works.

start with how screening prevents harm. the kit finds hidden blood, and a positive result leads to a closer look inside the bowel, where growths called polyps can be removed before they become cancer, or a cancer found early. so returning a kit is an impact measure: what people did, not yet what the disease did. now use the comparison. region a rose by nine percentage points, and region b, without the campaign, rose by two. so about seven points can be linked to the campaign.

now the data. thirteen of twenty is sixty-five per cent, against none of ten, and the untreated group strengthens the evidence that treatment caused the improvement. but it's a small trial, followed for one year, and it helps only people with this one gene fault, a small share of inherited blindness. it's very expensive, too. so it improved functional vision over one year for this gene fault, but the trial doesn't show the retina has stopped declining. it can't prevent inherited eye disease across a population.
